Stage 3 · Grammar

Which one, and by the way

One kind of clause tells you which one. The other just adds something.

Read these two sentences carefully.
  • The car that parks itself costs more than the standard model.
  • My car, which parks itself, cost more than I expected.
In which sentence could you delete the clause and still know which car is meant?
Two commas can change what a sentence means.

A relative clause gives extra information about a noun, joined to it by who, which, that, whose, where or when. English has two kinds, and although they look almost identical, they do completely different jobs. Recognising which one you are writing is the whole lesson.

A defining relative clause identifies which one you are talking about. It is essential: remove it and the listener no longer knows who or what you mean. Drivers who break the speed limit are fined refers only to that group of drivers. A non-defining relative clause adds extra detail about something that is already identified. Remove it and you still know exactly who is meant: My own disability, which I have had since birth, means I’ll never drive.

In writing, the comma is the only signal, and it genuinely changes the meaning. The cars which drive themselves are already on the road says that some cars — the self-driving ones — are on the road. The cars, which drive themselves, are already on the road says that all the cars in question drive themselves. In speech the same distinction is carried by a pause and a change of pitch.

From this single distinction, two practical rules follow. That is allowed only in defining clauses, never after a comma. And the relative pronoun can be left out only when it is the object of a defining clause (the car I bought), never when it is the subject (the car that broke down). One further point is worth flagging in advance because it survives to advanced levels: the relative pronoun already fills the object slot, so you must not repeat it — the car that I bought it.

One test decides everything. Delete the clause. If you still know who or what is meant, it is non-defining, so it takes commas. If you do not, it is defining, so no commas.

The commas change the meaning. My brother who lives in Almaty suggests I have more than one brother. My brother, who lives in Almaty, means I have one, and by the way he lives there.

The mistake to avoid. That is only for defining clauses: not My car, that parks itself, cost more but My car, which parks itself, cost more.

One more. Do not repeat the subject: not The man who he lives next door but The man who lives next door. The relative word is the subject.

Full grammar reference — relative clauses — defining and non-defining

What it is

A relative clause is a clause that gives information about a noun, joined to it by a relative pronoun: who, which, that, whose, where, when, why. English has two kinds, and they do completely different jobs. A defining relative clause identifies which one you mean and is essential. A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about something already identified, and could be removed without loss of identity.

What it means, and what it does

The comma is not decoration — it changes the meaning. The cars which drive themselves are already on the road says only the self-driving ones are. The cars, which drive themselves, are already on the road says all the cars in question drive themselves. In writing, the punctuation is the only thing telling your reader which you mean.

When and why we use it

A relative clause gives extra information about a noun, joined to it by who, which, that, whose, where or when. English has two kinds, and although they look almost identical, they do completely different jobs. Recognising which one you are writing is the whole lesson.

A defining relative clause identifies which one you are talking about. It is essential: remove it and the listener no longer knows who or what you mean. Drivers who break the speed limit are fined refers only to that group of drivers. A non-defining relative clause adds extra detail about something that is already identified. Remove it and you still know exactly who is meant: My own disability, which I have had since birth, means I’ll never drive.

In writing, the comma is the only signal, and it genuinely changes the meaning. The cars which drive themselves are already on the road says that some cars — the self-driving ones — are on the road. The cars, which drive themselves, are already on the road says that all the cars in question drive themselves. In speech the same distinction is carried by a pause and a change of pitch.

From this single distinction, two practical rules follow. That is allowed only in defining clauses, never after a comma. And the relative pronoun can be left out only when it is the object of a defining clause (the car I bought), never when it is the subject (the car that broke down). One further point is worth flagging in advance because it survives to advanced levels: the relative pronoun already fills the object slot, so you must not repeat it — the car that I bought it.

Typical situations

Relative clauses appear in every definition, every description of a person or a machine, every piece of technical writing, and any sentence where you need to combine two pieces of information about the same thing.

  • Identifying which one — a defining clause, no commas.Drivers who break the speed limit are fined automatically.
  • Adding extra detail — a non-defining clause, between commas.My own disability, which I have had since birth, means I’ll never drive a real car.
  • Talking about possession — whose, for people and often for things.People whose skills are better than the machines’ will still have work.
  • Talking about a place — where replaces in / at which.The junction where the accident happened has been redesigned.
  • Talking about a time — when replaces on / at which.2015 was the year when driverless cars first appeared in California.
  • Giving a reason — the reason why.That’s the reason why most of these accidents happen.
  • Commenting on a whole clause — which after a comma refers back to the entire idea.Many cars can already brake automatically, which means fewer collisions.

How it differs from similar structures

Defining (no commas) tells you which one; non-defining (commas) tells you something extra. Test it by deleting the clause: if you no longer know who or what is meant, it was defining.
who / which = the noun itself · whose = something belonging to the noun. the driver who has a licence vs the driver whose licence expired.

How to build it

Defining: noun + who / which / that + verb …  (no commas)
Non-defining: noun, + who / which + verb …,  (commas both sides)
Possession: noun + whose + noun + verb
Place / time: noun + where / when + subject + verb
Peoplewho (or that in defining clauses): the engineer who designed it
Things and animalswhich (or that in defining clauses): the device which controls the brakes
Possessionwhose: a driver whose licence has expired
Subject clausethe pronoun is the subject and cannot be left out: the car that drives itself
Object clausethe pronoun is the object and can be left out: the car (that) I bought
Non-definingonly who, which, whose, where, when — never that: Astana, which I visited last year,…
With a preposition, informalpreposition at the end: the lane which we were driving in
With a preposition, formalpreposition first, and then only whom / which: the lane in which we were driving

Usage notes and exceptions

  • That is impossible in a non-defining clause. My car, that is ten years old,… is always wrong. Use which.
  • You can leave the relative pronoun out only when it is the object of the defining clause: the car (that) I bought. If it is the subject, it must stay: the car that broke down.
  • Do not repeat the object pronoun: the car that I bought it. The relative pronoun already fills that slot — this is the most persistent error at B1.
  • Whom is the object form of who. In modern English it is required only directly after a preposition (the man to whom I spoke); otherwise who is normal.
  • Which after a comma can refer to a whole preceding clause: He arrived late, which annoyed everyone. What can never do this: …, what annoyed everyone.
  • In speech, non-defining clauses are marked by a pause and a change of pitch, exactly where the commas go in writing.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • The car that I bought it broke down. → The car that I bought broke down.Do not repeat the object — that already fills the slot.
  • My brother, that lives in Almaty, is a designer. → My brother, who lives in Almaty, is a designer.That cannot be used in a non-defining clause.
  • This is the man which helped me. → This is the man who helped me.Use who or that for people.
  • The village where I grew up in is tiny. → The village where I grew up is tiny. / The village which I grew up in is tiny.Where already contains the preposition.
  • He arrived late, what annoyed everyone. → He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.What cannot refer back to a clause.
  • The people who they work here are friendly. → The people who work here are friendly.Do not add a subject pronoun after the relative pronoun.

More examples in context

  • defining, subjectA driverless car is a car that can drive without a human at the wheel.
  • defining, objectThe app (which) I use tells me when the bus is late.
  • defining, peopleOnly people whose skills are better than the machines’ will still have work.
  • defining, placeThis is the junction where most of the accidents happen.
  • non-defining, personNeil Clough, who is our science correspondent, has been researching this.
  • non-defining, thingCloud seeding, which uses chemicals, has been around for decades.
  • non-defining, placeGeneva, where the laser research is being done, has a large university.
  • commenting on a clauseMany cars now brake automatically, which has cut low-speed collisions.
  • possessionThere’s a scientist whose experiments have shown that lasers can make rain.
  • formal prepositionThis is the possession for which I would never find a replacement.

A tip for remembering it

Say the sentence aloud. If you naturally pause before and after the clause, put commas in and never use that. If you say it straight through with no pause, leave the commas out and that is available. Then check the object rule: if you have already named the object once, you cannot name it again inside the clause.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Defining clauses identify which one and take no commas; non-defining clauses add extra detail and take commas.
  2. That is allowed only in defining clauses.
  3. The pronoun can be dropped only when it is the object of a defining clause.
  4. Never repeat the noun or pronoun inside the clause.
  5. Whose = possession; where = place; when = time; which after a comma can comment on a whole clause.
  6. In formal writing a preposition can go first, and then only whom or which follow it.

Stage 5 · Main input

The car that drives itself

The machines are already here. The argument is about something else.

Before you read: cars that drive themselves are already on the road in several countries.

What do you think is the hardest part for the engineers?

Choose one, then check Paragraph C.

The car that drives itself

The technology that removes the driver is already on the road. The hard part was never the driving.

AThere is a figure that appears in almost every discussion of driverless cars, and it explains why so much money has gone into them: around ninety per cent of road accidents are caused by human error. More than a million people die on the roads every year. A machine that never gets tired, never looks at its phone and never misjudges a gap at a junction would, in theory, remove most of that.

BMuch of the technology is already here, and you may be using it. Cars which brake automatically when the gap ahead closes are now ordinary. So are cars that park themselves, and systems which warn a driver who is slipping out of the correct lane on a motorway. Each of these does one job. What engineers call full automation — a vehicle that can handle any road, in any weather, with nobody paying attention — is a different problem altogether.

CThe difficulty is not the driving. It is the small number of situations that a human handles without noticing and a machine cannot. A ball rolls into the road, which usually means a child will follow. A police officer waves you through a red light. Two drivers arrive at a narrow gap at the same moment and settle it with a look. Engineers describe these as edge cases, and the awkward truth is that there is no complete list of them.

DFor some people the argument is already settled. Neil, who has had a disability since birth, will never take a driving test. “People talk about losing control,” he says. “I have never had it. A car that drives itself is the one possession that would change my week, and it is not replaceable by anything else. When people tell me the technology is not perfect yet, my answer is: neither is the system we have now.”

EThere are losses as well as gains, and they are not evenly shared. Driving is one of the most common paid occupations in many countries. If the vehicles that carry goods across a country no longer need a person in the cab, a large number of people whose skills are difficult to transfer will be looking for work. Some economists think new jobs will appear; others point out that they rarely appear in the same places, or for the same people.

FSo the question that matters is probably not whether the technology will arrive. It is what we decide to do while it does. The countries which are already writing rules for testing, insurance and responsibility will shape how it is used. The ones which wait will get whatever the manufacturers give them — which, as Neil points out, is roughly how the current system was built in the first place.

Written for this course. Collision-cause statistics and the levels-of-automation framework are drawn from published road-safety research and international engineering standards.
